30.history: Shipwrights of the smooth headland founded the harbour town on the south-eastern coast. In Dòmhnall Crùbach's reign the keepers of its waypoint houses took the gathering of the road toll into their own hands and paid the rìgh what they judged fair. His young niece Sìleas Dhonn, set to check their tallies, found three years in which their count did not match what had passed their gates. When the tallies came to be cut in the new marks, the keeper Ailig mac Ruairidh was checked against the road-guard's own cutting at his gate and found short by a sum no honest forgetting explained. In the twenty-ninth century fishers and carriers quarrelled here over who might carry dried fish up-country. Anna Ruadh ruled under the open sky that either might, and the fish going inland doubled.
30.known_for: the tallies that did not add, and the fish ruling

420.history: Settlers from Cathair dhomhain took the wet heath of the west coast in FE 879, where the soil is thin and the yellow scorpions thick. The town's oath began with a woman stung on the hand during a trade of cattle for salt fish, who finished the bargain with her fingers swelling and said a hurt taken in the open was worth more than a promise behind a closed door. Its people swore on a scorpion's sting kept in a box. Their neighbours thought it a strange custom, but merchants carried the sting-oath to Ros bheag, and in the last centuries every harbour court of the western coast swore by it.

36.history: The old harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine on the gulf was struck in FE 879 by a storm out of the west that drove the sea over it, took the boats at their moorings and a third of the houses, and left the survivors on the high ground with nothing but what they stood in. Coimheadaiche na Lasrach sent Talla na Lasrach's grain from Dùn ìseal and Dòmhnall Crùbach sent his from Dùn dhearg. The people of Seann Chwen ate from both that winter and never forgot which grain had come up the road first.
36.known_for: the storm and the two grains

1.history: The harbour on the wide strait grew rich on the western fishing and on the southern end of the carriers' road. At the end of the tenth century its leading family, under Lachlann Ciar, took the road toll for itself and sent none to Dùn dhearg. That brought on Cogadh nan Rathad, the first war since Loscadh Achadh mhòr. Iain Garbh shut the town in from the land for a season, but its boats fed it from the sea and the siege ended without an assault. Its men became its road-guards and swore their watch on a white stone carved as a wolf at the town gate, and Iain Garbh himself rode south to see it done. Lachlann Ciar died within sight of his harbour. In the twenty-ninth century the wolf-sworn raised a hall about the stone and swore graver oaths there.
1.known_for: the siege, and the wolf-stone at the gate

151.history: Carriers of the western road founded the town at the ford, and its toll-house, taken by Lachlann Ciar's men, was where Cogadh nan Rathad began in FE 999, when Iain Garbh burned it. His warband wintered on peat smoke in the burned house, and men who had marched south whole came home in spring with a cough some carried the rest of their days. The households resettled at the ford later grew a trading-meeting at Lùnastal, and Fearchar Òg's clerks granted it a charter. Mòrag Dhubh walked her wool there to trade.
151.known_for: the burned toll-house and the Lùnastal fair

500.history: Ford-keepers of the capital's country founded the crossing, where in FE 1,001 the men of Caol leathan met the levies of Iain Garbh and held the ford a day before they gave way. Forty lay dead of both sides, and the carriers call it Àth an Dà Fhichead. A man of Caol leathan held a split shield upright there well past any sense, until a spear from behind Iain Garbh's own rank found him. No name was kept for him.

45.history: Boat-households of An Cnoc Ruadh founded the lowland harbour. In FE 1,002 the men of Lachlann Ciar, falling back on Caol leathan, burned its granaries and standing grain so that the levies coming after would find nothing. Baile ghlas had sent Iain Garbh neither men nor grudge. Its people walked to Cathair dhomhain and to Baile chiar, and many never came back. The town was slowly rebuilt by those who did.
45.known_for: the town burned for another's war

106.history: The farming town south of the western bridge-foot shut its gate on both hosts in Cogadh nan Rathad and fed the burned-out people of Baile ghlas through the winter. When Iain Garbh rode up for a night's lodging, the reeve, Beathag, met him on the wall and would open to the hungry and to no one carrying a spear. He left his spear on the road and slept that night among refugees from a town he had ridden through the ashes of two days before. Neither side forgave Baile chiar, and neither attacked it.
106.known_for: the gate shut on both hosts

191.history: The salmon-trappers' harbour of the south-western shore sent its boats by night to feed besieged Caol leathan through Cogadh nan Rathad. In thanks Lachlann Ciar gave it a share of the western tolls, and with that the town raised the first stone harbour wall that coast had. Word of the wall reached Eithne's hall at Cathair mhòr with a wool-merchant.
191.known_for: the boats that fed the siege, and its harbour wall

17.history: The river port of the net-fishers on the Abhainn ghorm grew in the eleventh century on the trade that two new waypoint houses brought to it, until it outgrew every other northern town and asked Catrìona Ghlic for a road-guard of its own. It was given one without argument. It became the gathering-place of the northern wool trade, and the mountain sheep's fleece was woven here. A small harbour's headman once walked all the way to its fair to lay a complaint. By the last years of the age it held a wool-fair at every shearing, weighing its silver on the Muileann chiar weights.

212.history: The first millers of the northern river founded the town where the northern road comes over the pass. Its old waypoint keeper, Beathan mac Dhonnchaidh, recited his tally to Sìleas Dhonn from memory, name for name, and had no answer when she asked how she was to know it was the same tally he had given the road-guard three seasons before. A mill was raised in the twelfth century to grind the carriers' grain; the miller paid Talla na Lasrach in grain and the rìgh's toll in flour, and a town grew round the mill.
212.known_for: the mill on the pass and the old keeper's memory

393.history: The ford-keepers' town on the southern road toward Ceann leathan had its crossing's toll kept by the Griogaraich for longer than anyone could say. In FE 1,647 Fearchar Òg's clerks sent a hall-trained man, Dòmhnall Beag, to weigh the new silver toll there. For a year the ford's family would not help him, until firewood and floods brought them round to his scale. A toll-house was built and the road-guards were paid there in the new rings. In Falachd an Airgid two of its four guards left unpaid, and the keeper Oighrig nic Ailein stood the house through the winter. Grain came to her unnamed, and she guessed it was from Ruairidh Liath.
393.known_for: the first toll-keeper sent from the hall

354.history: Millers founded the town on the river bend up the valley from the landing at Cidhe Beag, and in the seventeenth century it became the home of the river-boatmen. Its young crews settled among themselves that no one might call himself one of their fellowship until he had sworn on his own paddle to answer another boat's call. Mòrag Dhubh's brother Dòmhnall swore his paddle here. Its yards built the flat hide boats for every river on the island.
354.known_for: the paddle-oath and the hide boats

22.history: The sailing households of the gulf made Ceann leathan the market of the southern fishing in the sixth century. Its harbour-master kept tallies on notched sticks, and dried fish went inland along the carriers' paths. The road-guards of the southern ford held their yearly meeting on its green, and in FE 1,665 Mòrag Dhubh of Cnoc mhòr won it by torchlight, the first woman to do so. Its traders asked Fearchar Òg's smiths for the ford's own mark on the season's finest ring. Anna Ruadh gave the green a stone-walled field and a ring from An Talla Dearg, and fed the losers at the crown's cost. Mòrag's ring, or one taken for hers, hangs by the green's well.

31.history: Cattle-drovers of the interior founded the town. Mòrag Dhubh was born here in FE 1,640 to Aonghas Ruadh, a guard of the southern ford paid in the first silver rings, and Sìne of Cnoc mhòr. She cut her own staff from a young ash at the wood's edge. Word of Fearchar Òg's death came down the southern road to her here in her age. Under Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte Cnoc mhòr raised its common granary before any other province seat, and Lachlann Bàn sent its reeve a silver ring for his own hand.
31.known_for: Mòrag Dhubh's town, and the first granary
